strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: explaining model behavior through interpretable concepts when only predictions and annotated inputs are available. The distinction between causal determinants and confounded associations has an identifiable audience in explainability, causal discovery, and algorithm auditing.

Under the stated causal and faithfulness assumptions, using PAGs is a principled way to represent latent confounding and uncertainty about causal direction. Applying established discovery tools to this setting is a worthwhile contribution without requiring a new algorithm.

The exposition provides helpful causal diagrams, an explicit structural model, and substantive discussion of identifiability, annotation availability, and measurement error. The simulation and two applications illustrate the workflow, while the alternative-algorithm analysis transparently reveals sensitivity.
weaknesses: Necessary: The empirical interpretation exceeds what the reported graph summaries establish. Section 6.3 pools directed and circle-arrow edges into one stability measure. A consistently recovered circle-arrow edge can remain compatible with purely confounded association; its stability does not establish that the feature is probably causal. Conversely, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal path through another feature. Statements in Section 6.4 and Figures 9–10 about likely causes and other features being causally irrelevant therefore need qualification. Separate definite causation, possible causation, and established non-causation, and consider paths when discussing ancestry.

Necessary: The Shapley counterexample in Section 3.3 and Appendix A does not establish the claimed confounding failure as written. Appendix A.2 holds the supposedly unobserved Z3 fixed and changes the empty-coalition baseline, replacing its cross-product expectation E[Z1 Z3] with z3 E[Z1]. This changes the attribution game rather than demonstrating the stated adjustment using only Z2. Moreover, if coalition values represent interventions on macro variables in the supplied SCM, Appendix A.1 must account for changes in descendant Z1 when intervening on Z2 or Z3. Define a consistent estimand and rederive the comparison, or remove this purported demonstration.

Necessary: The X-ray sampling scheme needs a causal justification. Selecting pneumonia cases and controls with 'no findings' makes inclusion depend jointly on disease and the explanatory findings. Such selection can introduce dependencies that are not addressed merely by allowing latent confounding, and the paper explicitly sets selection effects aside. Explain why the proposed causal interpretations remain valid under this sampling scheme, provide an appropriate analysis, or restrict these results to exploratory findings.

Necessary: The reliability of the real-data conditional-independence tests is insufficiently documented. The X-ray analysis has only 240 images with potentially rare findings; the bird analysis conditions on combinations of several multilevel attributes. Report relevant cell counts, handling of sparse contingency tables, and exactly which training or held-out observations enter structure learning. Bootstrap stability cannot repair poorly calibrated tests. The substantial change from Wing Shape/Wing Pattern/Tail Shape under FCI to Crown Color/Size under GRaSP-FCI also limits the strength of the bird-specific conclusions. Suitable validation or narrower empirical claims are needed; clinical or visual plausibility alone does not validate causal recovery.

Optional: Paired interventions in the synthetic image generator and repeated graph-recovery experiments would clarify finite-sample performance and whether the learned image detectors introduce unintended dependencies. A comparison using the same concept annotations with a simple association-based explanation would also help isolate the benefit of causal discovery. The current LIME/SHAP examples mainly illustrate differences in explanatory representation.
